planting.note: Set dormant rhizome sections just below the soil surface in early spring in moist, humus-rich woodland soil in part sun to shade, where the colony will slowly widen by underground runners.

directions: This selection of the native American mayapple was collected from a southern population and distinguishes itself from typical wild mayapple by its pleasantly fragrant white flowers, held just beneath the umbrella-like leaves in very early spring. New foliage unfurls with coppery bronze patterning before settling into deep green through the growing season. Like the species, it spreads steadily by shallow rhizomes to form a dense woodland groundcover and goes fully dormant by midsummer. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich soil in part sun to shade for the best long-term colony growth.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizome divisions shallowly in rich, consistently moist woodland soil in part shade to full shade in early spring, before leaves have expanded.

directions: This clone belongs to forma deamii, a naturally occurring color variant of the American mayapple first found in Indiana, distinguished from the ordinary white-flowered, yellow-fruited species by pale pink blooms and purple-flushed stems, leaf stalks, and fruit. The deeply lobed leaves still emerge in pairs atop each flowering stem and carry a light brownish flush as they unfurl in early spring. Like the straight species it spreads gradually by shallow rhizomes into a dense woodland colony and disappears completely by midsummer dormancy. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in shade to part shade, where it makes an unusual talking-point addition to a native woodland planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich woodland soil in part shade to shade, keeping newly set plants consistently moist until established.

directions: A hybrid between the Asian species Podophyllum delavayi and Podophyllum versipelle, this selection emerges each spring with chocolate-brown foliage that gradually mottles with olive green and cinnamon tones as the leaves mature. Large nodding red flowers are held beneath the foliage in spring and the clump often produces a light second flush of bloom in fall. It grows noticeably more compact and dense than either parent species, making it easier to place in a smaller shaded border than some of the larger-leaved Asian mayapples. Provide humus-rich, evenly moist soil and part to full shade, and divide congested clumps after a few years of establishment.
